summary: Deep-dive on throughput tuning for Peregrine's on-prem private deployment. Focus areas: pipeline tiling (slice-level packing), prefetch window sizing to warm KV cache, eviction strategy tradeoffs under peaky loads, and upper token caps/max_num_seqs interactions with continuous batching. Discussed conservative vs aggressive prefetch profiles, suggested scheduler knobs and safe rollout steps. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share configs + scripts; Peregrine to run benchmarks and reconvene.
topics: KV cache prefetch sizing and warmup
eviction policies (LRU vs LFU vs size-based)
interplay of max_num_seqs and token limits with continuous batching
on-prem VPC networking effects on cold-starts
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: ok hey everyone thanks for joining from Peregrine, this is Alex from Redwood, we have Priya and Diego from our side, how's the time on your end?
[00:05] Jesse Tran: yep all good, afternoon here, thanks for doing this, we wanted to focus on throughput tuning - we've hit some weird tail latency spikes when burts come in.
[00:12] Alex Morgan: right yeah so goal for today is a sanity check on your scheduler knobs and prefetch profile, walk through tiling approach, and make a concrete plan to run a bench. sound good?
[00:20] Lena Ortiz: sounds good - we also want to avoid any config that would blow up memory on our shard nodes.
[00:25] Priya Raman: cool, I'm going to share a rough diagram - (slight pause) - ok picture: requests enter gateway -> router -> continuous batcher -> pipeline-tiler which groups sequences into slices -> inference engines with KV cache. Tiling reduces padding by grouping similar length sequences, but it interacts with max_num_seqs in the scheduler.
[00:42] Samira Bello: when you say tiling are you talking about fixed-size slices or dynamic tiling based on seq length histogram?
[00:47] Priya Raman: dynamic. we compute histogram over recent window and create variable slice sizes - smaller for long-tail lengths. That keeps throughput high but can cause more eviction churn in KV cache if prefetch window is too small.
[01:02] Markus Hsu: can you clarify prefetch window? is that number of next-token entries you prewarm?
[01:07] Diego Chen: yeah it's effectively how far ahead the scheduler asks the runtime to warm kv cache / pre-compile kernels for sequences in a slice. we call it prefetch-window. setting it to 0 is cold; 100 is aggressive warm.
[01:18] Jesse Tran: we tried prefetch-window=500 in dev and saw memory spike and occasional OOMs on 80GB nodes, which is why Lena's worried.
[01:25] Priya Raman: that's expected. prefetch-window multiplies by average token length per seq and number of seqs in a tile; so if you tile aggressively you need to cap max_num_seqs or reduce prefetch window.
[01:36] Lena Ortiz: also our workload has spikes where 70% of requests are short (<=64) but a small fraction are long 512-1024. the long ones evict a lot.
[01:45] Alex Morgan: ok typical mixed workload. two knobs we suggest: 1) slice-aware prefetch: only prefetch for slices composed primarily of short sequences; 2) soft token caps per-tenant to limit worst-case memory.
[01:58] Samira Bello: soft token caps meaning we return 429 for requests that would exceed token budget?
[02:03] Priya Raman: soft caps prefer graceful degrade: re-route to smaller model variant or enqueue with lower priority rather than immediate 429. you can do token ceiling heuristics (per-request predicted tokens) and accept until a threshold.
[02:15] Jesse Tran: that could help. what about eviction - we are seeing LRU performing poorly because hot short sequences get evicted by big long ones.
[02:24] Diego Chen: we recommend a size-aware LRU/LFU hybrid - track access frequency but weight by sequence length footprint. LFU with aging to avoid stale hot items dominating.
[02:34] Lena Ortiz: do you have a reference config?
[02:36] Priya Raman: yes I'll attach a sample. rough safe defaults for on-prem 80GB GPU: prefetch-window=100 for short-slice, prefetch-window=16 for long-slice; max_num_seqs=32 for mixed tiling; token-cap-per-request=4096; eviction=size-weighted-lfu with aging factor 0.9.
[02:56] Markus Hsu: why max_num_seqs 32? we were running 64 before.
[02:59] Priya Raman: 64 increases KV memory linearly because the batch contains more KV entries; it also increases padding if tiling isn't perfect. moving to 32 keeps steady-state memory under control and still allows decent throughput. you can bump to 48 if you have headroom and use a conservative prefetch.
[03:13] Jesse Tran: curious about continuous batching latency tail - how does tiling affect tail?
[03:19] Alex Morgan: tiling helps average token utilization but can introduce stragglers when a slice contains one very long sequence; scheduler has options: max_seq_delta_per_slice which caps the difference between shortest/longest seq in a tile. set that to 128 to avoid mixing 64 and 1024.
[03:34] Samira Bello: ok that seems smart. does that hurt throughput?
[03:36] Diego Chen: small hit on throughput for worst-case, but long sequences are relatively rare so overall better tail. also combine with admission-control to smooth bursts: e.g., token-bucket or concurrency-window.
[03:47] Jesse Tran: admission control - we had poor user experience when requests queued for too long. any recommended SLOs?
[03:52] Priya Raman: we suggest a soft latency SLO for enqueue < 200ms 95th under normal load, and use progressive fallback: start enqueuing to lower-tier pool after 150ms, and after 500ms route to smaller model variant.
[04:06] Lena Ortiz: let's talk prefetch sizing more - you suggested 100 for short-slice earlier. how do we pick that empirically?
[04:12] Priya Raman: run a ramp test: start prefetch=0 then step 16,32,64,100,150 while running a synthetic mixed-histogram workload for 30m each. measure KV hit rate, GPU memory, tail latency. pick smallest prefetch that reaches >85% KV hit without memory spike.
[04:26] Jesse Tran: ok we can run that. what about quantization interactions - we quantize to int8 and sometimes see kernels slowdowns on long sequences after prefetch.
[04:35] Diego Chen: quantization can change kernel selection; some int8 kernels have different perf characteristics at high seq lengths. recommendation: measure per-kernel throughput across seq lengths; we have scripts to autotune kernel selection per model and sequence length profile. i'll share them.
[04:48] Markus Hsu: there's a line in our infra where VPC egress to internal model store adds 20-40ms cold overhead - is that relevant to prefetch?
[04:55] Alex Morgan: yes if prefetch triggers downloads/hotload from model store, network latency can kill warmup efficiency. two mitigations: co-locate model shards and use aggressive prefetch for short slices only, or use a small local on-node disk cache to avoid repeated remote fetch.
[05:09] Lena Ortiz: we don't have local SSD on all nodes. can't change infra quickly.
[05:12] Priya Raman: then be conservative with prefetch and focus on improving KV hit via slice affinity - try to route requests from same customer to same worker for a warmup corridor. this uses soft-sharding.
[05:24] Jesse Tran: interesting - we have sticky routing for sessions but not for stateless requests. could add sticky headers.
[05:29] Alex Morgan: ok next piece: safe rollout plan to change knobs. we recommend canary 1% traffic for 1 hour with metrics watchlist (GPU mem, KV hit, 95/99 latency), then 10% for 3 hours, then 100% if stable. also keep automatic fallback to previous config on OOM or 99th latency regress > 20%.
[05:50] Samira Bello: what about continuous batching parameters - we use batch-window=20ms, max_batch_tokens=8192. are those reasonable?
[05:57] Diego Chen: batch-window 20ms is aggressive but fine for low-latency; combine with max_batch_tokens and max_num_seqs so you don't accumulate giant batches in traffic spikes. for your mix maybe max_batch_tokens=12000 and max_num_seqs=32.
[06:11] Jesse Tran: we have a case where a malformed client sends extremely long context and stalls pipeline. any defensive measures?
[06:18] Priya Raman: enforce per-request max_context_tokens at the gateway and validate predicted generation length; also token ceilings and pre-parse to reject obviously malicious payloads.
[06:28] Lena Ortiz: ok good. quick question - are there interactions between eviction policy and metrics we should watch beyond KV hit and memory?
[06:36] Alex Morgan: yes track eviction churn (evictions per minute), average access age, and miss re-pop latency. also watch GPU utilization variance - if eviction churn correlates with sudden dips in utilization you know it's thrashing.
[06:48] Jesse Tran: can Redwood provide a Grafana dashboard template for these?
[06:51] Priya Raman: yes we'll send a dashboard with panels for KV hit, evictions/min, avg access age, GPU mem, 95/99 latencies, batch sizes distribution.
[06:59] Markus Hsu: earlier you mentioned size-weighted LFU with aging factor - can you explain briefly how aging factor works?
[07:05] Diego Chen: aging factor decays counters periodically to give recent accesses more weight; for example multiply counters by 0.9 every 10s. avoids permanent hotspots from historic popularity.
[07:15] Samira Bello: that should help. any gotchas for on-prem vs hosted?
[07:19] Priya Raman: on-prem you usually have less headroom and network variability, so conservative prefetch, lower max_num_seqs, and stronger admission control. hosted can be more aggressive with prefetch and higher max_num_seqs due to abundant memory and scale-out fallback.
[07:34] Jesse Tran: perfect. what's the expected improvement we might see with these changes?
[07:38] Alex Morgan: depends, but typical customers see 10-25% throughput uplift while reducing 99th latency by 20-40% in mixed workloads if they tune prefetch and max_num_seqs together.
[07:47] Lena Ortiz: that's promising. ok let's recap next steps.
[07:50] Alex Morgan: recap: Priya will share sample configs, prefetch ramp script, and Grafana dashboard. Jesse will run ramp with steps (0,16,32,64,100,150) for short/long slice profiles and upload traces. Diego will share kernel auto-tune scripts for quantized kernels. we'll do follow-up 30m after Peregrine uploads results.
[08:08] Jesse Tran: yep will aim to start bench tomorrow. thanks everyone.
[08:12] Alex Morgan: thanks all, meeting adjourn.
